Customs tariff-410c.	(i) Machinery and
apparatus and complete parts thereof for use exclusively in producing unrefined oil from shales, not to include motive power, of a class or kind not made in Canada: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
(ii) Machinery and apparatus for operating oil-sands by mining operations and for extracting oil from the sands so mined; complete parts of the foregoing:	British preferential tariff,
free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.	[DOT]

Both parts of this item have to do with the importation of machinery for the development of the oil
44501-267J
resources of Canada, but one has reference to machinery for producing unrefined oil from shale, while the other has to do with the production of oil from tar sands in western Canada. I notice in this item that the machinery for producing oil from shale is free of duty except for the motive power in the machines. With a war on, and with such dire necessity for oil in this country, I see no reason why there should be any tariff whatever on any machinery that can be used for developing the oil resources of Canada at this time. Even if it is an engine that goes into the machine, we are not going to interfere with anyone making engines in Canada to-day merely because we permit the free importation of an engine for an oil drilling machine of any type. Engines are so hard to obtain now that you must get priorities before you can obtain them. All this oil drilling machinery and all material used for the development of oil, such as pipe, drilling machines, bit stems, bits, refining machinery, and so on, should be allowed in duty free from any country in which we can get them, in order to develop our oil resources.
Much has been said by leaders throughout the democratic part of this world in the last few months about freeing the channels of trade throughout the world when the war is over, in order that all democratic countries may have access to raw materials and may trade with other countries in order that there may be a fuller life throughout this whole world. If we are ever to get at that at all, it is time we were getting at it now. If there is one thing for which I have to criticize the Minister of Finance in connection with this budget it is that in it he has made no move toward that end. If we cannot have some of these restrictive tariffs removed now, when there is no necessity in the world for them, when this war is over it will be even more difficult to do it. To-day we are more and more industrializing one certain part of Canada. By the time the war is over that part of Canada will be so highly industrialized that they will fight every move that is made to reduce tariffs, and the result will be that other parts of Canada will suffer even more than they have suffered in the past.
They are suffering now.

It is therefore
about time the government made some real reductions in tariffs in order to start this thing going. It is recognized that the sentiment of the people, in this country, in Great Britain, and in the United States of America, has changed greatly in regard to trade matters. A majority in all these countries is of the opinion that trade between the democratic nations of the world should be unfettered.
Customs Tariff

I repeat, I do not know how we are going to be able to do anything about it after the war if we are not ready to do it now. Therefore I am sorry that this budget has not provided for drastic reductions in the tariff.
I think something should be said by hon. members with a view to seeing that those changes are made when the next budget comes down. Is it not ridiculous that Canada, a highly industrialized country, which is giving to Great Britain the greater part of a billion dollars in war goods manufactured in this country, for the purpose of helping her and ourselves in this war, and deferring until after the war the repayment of a loan of some $700,000,000, should be sending these goods to Great Britain in that way because it is impossible for Great Britain to pay for them in goods?

Is it not
part of our contribution to the common effort, not a gift at all?

No doubt part
of it is.

What has it to do with
this item?

It has this to do with it, that even if Great Britain wanted to pay with goods, we, the Canadian people, through our tariffs, are saying, "No; your goods cannot come into this country, even to help pay your debt to us." That is a ridiculous situation and should be corrected.
I have spoken here before for freer trade, and I intend to keep on doing it. I think this country and the world at large is at last beginning to see the light of that kind of reasoning, and I hope the Minister of Finance will be able to see some more of it before the next budget.

I am greatly surprised
that the minister has seen fit to place such an enormous tax upon "machinery and apparatus for operating oil sands by mining operations and for extracting oil from the sands so mined, and complete parts of the foregoing." Thirty-five per cent is a tremendous tax on that machinery at a time when the people of this country are anxious to develop our oil resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not putting it on; I
am taking it off.
Well, take it completely off-that is what I ask. Perhaps the minister might explain what this is. There seems to be some confusion.

The confusion is at
your end. It is free. You do not want anything better than that.

I do not read anything
free there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have before me two
columns, on page 16 of the ways and means resolutions. The first column contains the proposals; the second column-which is divided into three parts, as is the first- contains the present rates. The present rates for certain of these articles are, free, 27i per cent, and 35 per cent; and for others, 10, 27i, and 35 per cent. All these duties are being removed and the articles placed on the free list under all classifications.

Then I shall have to
make the same speech but instead of castigating the minister I shall have to compliment him. The fact of the matter is that we in Canada are anxiously trying to develop our oil resources. This item will apply particularly to the Fort McMurray tar sand development, in which we in this corner of the house are particularly interested. The development of these sands will aid tremendously the building of the Alaska highway, and that highway will aid greatly the defences of that northern territory. In my study of this matter I find that one of the obstacles encountered is that it is difficult to mine those sands and extract the oil in competition with oil obtained from drilled wells. This will help the tar sand producers to compete.
I was pleased to hear the Minister of Munitions and Supply say not long ago that they are sending men in there to review this whole situation and bring about further development of the Fort McMurray tar sands. I urge upon him that he do this speedily. Let the government develop them, or give every possible inducement to their development, without delay.
Will the tariff be removed on rotary drilling rigs such as those used in deep drilling in Turner Valley, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Item 410d, which was inserted last year, provides that the following shall be duty free:
Well-drilling machinery and apparatus, and complete parts thereof, for use exclusively in drilling for water, natural gas or oil, or in prospecting for minerals, not to include motive power; machinery and apparatus of a class or kind not made in Canada for maintenance and testing purposes in connection with gas or oil wells; well-packers and complete parts thereof, for oil or gas wells; seamless iron or steel tubing of a class or kind not made in Canada, for use in casing water, natural gas or oil wells.
That does not exempt the motive power used in drilling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct.

Customs Tariff
Is there any reason why it should not be exempted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know of any. That is the question that was raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I have made inquiries to ascertain whether there have been any communications or complaints with regard to diesel engines and the like. I find there have not, and it is now a little late to suggest that in connection with this budget.
Then could it be considered for next year's budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it can be considered. There may be reasons against it which I do not know, but we have not considered it; that is all.

I understand that what is being done in this item is to restore a position which previously obtained, from 1936 to 1938, in connection with the United States trade agreement. In the new agreement of 1938 the arrangement was dropped and is now being revived. It is not a new proposal at all, except with reference to a portion coming under the intermediate and general tariffs. Everything is to be made free. This machinery and apparatus for use exclusively in producing unrefined oil from shale, for instance, is of a class or kind not made in Canada. It is intended, I think, to help in the development of the oil shales of New Brunswick and eastern Canada generally; that is part 1. Part 2 is to help in the development of the oil sands. Part 1 does not include the motive power, which I understand is of a class or kind made in Canada, and the protection heretofore given on that is being continued. I see no great objection to the passing of this item as it is, if we understand the position historically and what is now being sought. I have an idea that previously it was all one item and it is now being separated. In any event all this machinery and apparatus, which is of a class or kind not made in Canada, is being put on the free list. That is in accordance with government policy; I am not objecting to it, and I think we might carry the item.

The minister is to be commended for removing the duty on this apparatus, because this may tend to increase the production of oil in areas where oil is contained in the shale and tar sands. But I do not think the results for which we hope will come about simply through the removal of this duty. The government should go further. I realize that the Minister of Finance is not concerned in what I
am about to say, but I think our endeavours to develop the present production of oil from all sources, including the tar sands and the shale, should be greatly increased. The government should go much further than merely removing the duty on this equipment, because the situation is becoming exceedingly critical.
I brought up this question in the house over a year ago, but up to the present time practically nothing has been done to develop the production of oil from our tar sands. I am sure the minister recognizes the seriousness of our oil situation just as much as anyone else, probably more so than a great many people in this country. We see now that the oil fields of Iraq and Iran are in a very dangerous position; in fact the entire Persian field is in a most critical situation, and according to information appearing in the public press the United States is becoming acutely aware of an oil shortage in that country. A great deal of our crude oil comes from the-United States; and when we see them going to the extent of setting up plants for the production of synthetic oil from coal, it becomes apparent that the situation is serious. We in Canada are favourably situated in that regard; we have the largest potential oil field in the world, bar none. Right now, when the situation is so critical, when the possibility of having our supply of oil from the Persian field cut off is becoming more apparent day by day, the government and the Minister of Finance should insist that the development of these oil fields be hurried along as much as possible.
The minister will remember that when I brought up this question in the early part of 1941 I was ridiculed; I was called a defeatist and an alarmist when I dared to suggest that before this war was over our oil supply from Iraq and Iran might be cut off. I am not satisfied with the progress that has been made, and I want to commend the Minister of Finance on the removal of the duty from this equipment, which may hasten our progress in this direction. Certainly I am not satisfied with the progress that has been made in the development of the tar sands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Operations are going on at the moment, I am told.

Just in an
experimental way, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so.

When I spoke on this matter previously the Minister of Munitions and Supply took me to task and said that the prospect of developing oil from the tar sands was too remote for this war, that perhaps we would have it for the next

war. I am glad to note that once more the Minister of Munitions and Supply has been forced to change his opinion. Perhaps the Minister of Finance has had to sit on him a little; and if that has brought about the good results shown here I hope the minister sits on him good and hard, so that some real action may be taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sitting on him.

Under this item is
machinery to be admitted free for the removal from the oil sands of bitumen and other ingredients, or merely the oil?

While my colleague is looking up the information I might just say, for the information of the hon. member for Bow River, that I have ascertained by inquiry that final investigations of the McMurray and Waterways district are in progress at the present time, looking toward the actual production of oil from those sands. I do not know how far the minister concerned may care to go in giving details of arrangements that have been made, but I can assure the hon. member that this work is definitely under way.

Then may I ask the minister whether he will consider the advisability of setting up a committee of this house when parliament reassembles to make a thorough investigation of 'the progress being made in the development of oil from these tar sands, as well as developments in the manufacture of synthetic rubber in Canada. If the minister will give the committee that assurance I think it would be to the advantage of our war effort.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I am the minister to whom the hon. member refers, all I can say is that I will bring what he has said to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Munitions and. Supply.
Replying to the question of the hon. member for Davenport, this item provides for the free entry of "machinery and apparatus for operating oil-sands by mining operations and for extracting oil from the sands so mined." His question was whether machinery for extracting other substances-
Such as bitumen and tar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -from the sands so mined will be admitted free. Such machinery is not covered by the item. I do not know enough about machinery to know whether the machinery provided with free entry by this item could be used for both purposes. If not, it is not covered.

I was hoping this item would go through. May I ask the minister whether any machinery is to be imported for the development of the oil shales, and whether there have been any developments with respect to the oil shales in New Brunswick. Months ago I brought to the attention of the oil controller the position in New Brunswick, and I was met with the statement that it was not part of government policy to go into the production business itself. I can understand that. Then I urged that investigations should be made, and I was promised that some investigation would be made. What I am asking now is whether investigations have taken place, how far have they proceeded, and is there any prospect of the development of the oil shales of New Brunswick, which are known to be a substantial natural resource of that part of the country, where we need development if we can possibly get it.
I am not deprecating what the minister is doing by this item. This machinery is not made in Canada, and was admitted free some years ago. I think there is some differentiation, and I was hoping that the minister would give the history of the position, which I attempted to give somewhat inadequately a few moments ago. This item is not a new departure. It simply restores the item to the position which obtained up to 1938, at which time the item was dropped.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From 1936 to 1938, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
With reference to the point raised by the leader of the opposition, I think I announced to the house that the federal government, in partnership with the provincial government, was making a very thorough investigation of the oil shales of New Brunswick. The investigation is practically completed, but I have not seen the final report. An interim report which I saw indicated not too hopeful a situation. The shales did not have the oil content that it was hoped would be found.
As regards the Alberta tar sands, we are making a very thorough investigation. We are not only checking all available data, but are making a close examination of refinery results in that area. We are having refinery runs made of the product, as well as laboratory tests, and we are drilling to find the extent of the sands with a view to a large scale development. In both cases I think we are taking the steps which are necessary before large expenditures would be warranted.

Would the Minister of
Munitions and Supply enlarge upon the statement he made on May 15 with respect to this

There were only two plants operating in the oil sand area. There was the bitumen plant, forty or fifty miles north of Fort McMurray, operated by Mr. Fitzsimmons, and they were doing a pretty good job in extracting bitumen. They were shipping thousands of barrels of bitumen and tar. When I was up there last summer I saw two hundred barrels going up the river. The other plant, which was manufacturing oil, was turning out a year ago somewhere between 200 and 250 barrels a day, but unfortunately the plant was burned down in the fall. It has been rebuilt, and the last information I had was that before now the rebuilt plant should be turning out about 600 barrels a day.
I am in accord with this item, which is to admit free the machinery required for the further development of these sands. All the machinery used in the oil plants came from the United States, and there is not a great deal of it even there. This machinery requires constant replacement; so that if this item, which will admit free machinery not made in Canada which is required for extracting the oil from the oil sands, will assist in the development of these sands, I think we should all be in favour of it.

I was not in the house on Monday when the debate on the excise resolutions took place with regard to the taxing of alcoholic beverages. I was attending a committee meeting. Had I been here I should have liked to say a few words on this important question, and perhaps I may be allowed to say them now; this is * somewhat similar resolution.
Customs Tariff

I would urge that measures be taken to cut down the further use of such intoxicants, because it seems to me there are no factors that contribute more to the inefficiency, the degradation and the sorrows of individuals and of the nation, than the continued abuse of physical, moral and mental powers through the use of intoxicating liquor. It is a waste of human and material resources. I do not want to reopen the debate that took place on Monday, but I feel bound to say a few words on this subject. I have sometimes thought seriously of introducing a resolution which I might ask any of the hon. gentlemen who spoke on Monday, and who applauded temperance sentiments, to support. It may be that reform in this case is hard to obtain by legislation.	The experience
of the prohibition years shows the difficulty of attempting to keep men sober by law- or women either-but I think it should be our responsibility to educate our young people in the danger of the use of alcoholic beverages, danger to body, mind and soul. Boys and girls should be told of the misery they are storing up for themselves, how they undercut their God-given abilities and prodigally throw away- their opportunities right and left when they give these and similar poisons a chance to do their work. They should know that drinking is the preliminary step along the primrose path that leads to disease, crime and destruction.
I am not going to make a speech; I am simply offering a couple of suggestions that might be valuable to the minister and to temperance societies. It seems to me that the temperance societies are not making much headway towards legislation for absolute prohibition. In Sweden before the war they had a different method of approaching the control of alcohol than by resorting to absolute prohibition. I will not go into that, but you will find it set out in Marquis Child's book, "Sweden-The Middle Way," chapter 8, on "Liquor Control That Works." Another suggestion I would make is that in addition to taxes and tariffs we might label every bottle containing alcohol with some such inscription as this; it was written by an eminent physician. May I read it: Directions for Use
Use moderately and not on successive days. Eat well while drinking. If necessary, supplement food with vitamin tablets while drinking.
W arning
May be habit-forming. Not for use by children. If this beverage is indulged in immoderately it may cause intoxication (drunkenness), later neuralgia and paralysis (neuritis), and serious mental derangement, such as delirium tremens and other curable and incurable mental diseases, as well as kidney and liver damage.
[Mrs. Casselman.l
If this were used as an advertisement in newspapers or on street cars it might serve a more useful purpose than some of the advertisements we have seen, and it might counteract certain advertisements which were spoken of on Monday by some hon. members, put out by different firms that deal in such beverages. We should increase taxes and tariffs and warn all and sundry of the deadly dangers they run.

Have the minister and the administration taken cognizance of the public reaction to the debate on Monday in this house, and has the government given consideration to steps which would have the effect of diminishing the huge sums of money now diverted to the liquor trade in this country? I think the minister would find, if he read the press across Canada, that for the most part the expression of opinion from either side of the house on Monday last has been well received. I will not repeat in any measure what I said on that occasion, and I am not inviting another debate on the question, but I should like to know whether the government has considered the reaction of public opinion in regard to this matter. Will the administration make some effort to negotiate with-the provincial administrations with respect to the huge increase in the retail sales of liquor? Since we met the other day I have had occasion to review what Mr. MacMillan, the premier of Nova Scotia said, in the legislature, I believe, with reference to the huge increase in sales in that province. He affirmed the position that among the civilian population the increase has not been large, but that the increase, in his view at all events, was due to two factors, namely, the large increase in the sales in the city of Halifax arising from the fact that so many ships were entering and leaving that port, and also the position with respect to sales in the vicinity of the large army camp at Debert. I hope the government will not leave all the responsibility with the provincial governments. There is a responsibility on the federal government to do something in the matter. Various methods have been suggested. I am not going into them now, but I think we ought to cut down this bill with respect to spirits by at least one-third between now and the next budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not had time to read the editorials on the subject since last Monday. In fact the only one I saw was not in accord with what the hon. gentleman has said; it was the other way. But probably the others will come in, and I shall see them sooner or later. I think it would be a most

Customs Tariff
serious step for this government to be responsible for instituting a system of dual responsibility for the control of the liquor traffic in Canada. The moment we start that we are in for plenty of trouble. Everything that goes wrong is then the fault of the other jurisdiction.

Yesterday a return for which I had moved was brought down, in connection with statutes that have been amended, suspended or otherwise interfered with by order in council. Apparently so far as statutes are concerned the government has seen fit to amend them in a great many ways under the powers contained in the War Measures Act. I think that generally speaking all over Canada to-day there is a feeling that something should be done toward reducing the increasing consumption of intoxicating liquors. Apparently the government does not feel disposed to use the powers it has under the War Measures Act to reduce this consumption. If it will not use those powers, does it not think that a national appeal should be made by the government to people all over Canada, in the interests of an increasing war effort, to reduce their private consumption of intoxicating liquors? That I think the government could do. It could prevent the advertising of intoxicating liquors. During part of the period from 1929 to 1934 the government of Saskatchewan refused to permit liquor advertising in that province. It was criticized for interfering with private business. The result of the refusal to permit the advertising of liquor was not apparent until after that ban had been removed, when there was an immediate and very considerable increase in consumption, in no way attributable to increase in population, the process being rather in the other direction.
Having regard to the feeling of people all over this country, will the government give consideration, if not to the use of its powers, to a national appeal to the people of Canada urging upon them, in the interests of the war effort, that they reduce the private consumption of intoxicating liquors?

I should like to add
a word to what has been said on this subject. I do not know what effect a national appeal would have, but the government has the power, and from all parts of this house expressions of opinion have come from hon. members representing all shades of opinion that the consumption of intoxicating liquor since the war began has increased to an alarming extent. When we are not only asking but conscripting young men to join the armed forces, we ought to see to it at least that the
fears which naturally arise among the parents of those boys are allayed so far as we are able to allay them.
I know that we tried prohibition in the last war and the experiment did not work out as many of us who supported the prohibition campaign at that time believed it would, and perhaps we could not enforce a measure of prohibition at this time. But every possible effort should be made in that direction, not only by appealing to the population of the country to reduce the consumption of intoxicating liquor, but by the government restricting the hours of sale, perhaps rationing the amount supplied, and generally endeavouring to cut down the consumption of intoxicating liquor, or at least its widespread sale in places where it is easily accessible to young men who often in their periods of rest have little chance of recreation other than in some sort of beer parlour.
I strongly endorse the sentiments which have been expressed and the requests that have been made of the government. I have sufficient faith in the government to believe that it will consider the matter and take effective steps to remove what has become a real menace to many of our people.

I have one suggestion to make to the minister. I realize his difficulty and how reluctant he would be to interfere with the trade by way of prohibition. But it is a well-known fact that the greater amount of drinking takes place in the later hours of the evening and on into the small hours of the morning. My suggestion would be that the wartime prices and trade board should restrict the hours of sale. Ten o'clock in the evening is late enough. Those of us who have been in Ottawa many months have witnessed the scenes mentioned' by one hon. member the other evening as having occurred1 on Bank street and other streets in * the city between eleven and twelve o'clock at night. A reduction of hours of sale might not stop these incidents, but I believe would curtail consumption to a considerable extent. The wartime prices and trade board are curtailing the liberty of the subject in every other way; why should they hesitate to do it in a matter affecting the moral welfare of the people?
I should like to have an answer from the minister as to the attitude of the government towards such a national campaign as I have suggested.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It must be remembered that if we were to take direct curtailment measures, the body being curtailed would be the crown in the right of the province, because the crown in the right of the province, in every province with the exception of Prince Edward Island, I think, controls as a monopoly the sale of liquor. What we are being asked to do in taking such measures is to step right into the field of another jurisdiction being actively exercised at the moment, and say to that jurisdiction: "You are not doing your duty; this is what you shall do hereafter."
I do not think this government is the guardian of the morals of the people to any greater extent than the governments of the provinces, and I have never been able to see why pressure converged upon this government. The people who are in the business, who have a monopoly of the sale, and who are sovereign, under the decisions, within their jurisdiction to the same extent that the federal government is-they have all the powers in the world in this particular matter. If they are exercising them wrongly, why do they not exercise them properly? It is part of the war effort of the provinces; it is something they should do; it is their responsibility; it is their duty, and they should discharge it. Speeches such as we have heard here are all to the good as a manifestation of a very considerable popular sentiment in the country; but do not try to push this government into a position which the prov-in'ces now occupy.
The federal government put in prohibition during the last war.

While it is true that the provincial governments are very largely interested in the liquor business-I think unfortunately, from many points of view- I believe that ultimately the only way to control the entire liquor traffic will be to take it out of private hands altogether and, under rigid government supervision, handle the whole business from the manufacture right down to the sale. The manufacturers 
and distillers of liquor are the people who are making huge fortunes out of it. I can think of one fortune in this country, for example, which began in a little junk yard in the city of Regina during the last war. Its foundations were laid through one of the most pernicious bootlegging businesses this country has ever seen, with hi-jacking and similar practices of every description. To-day the people who were associated with that little junk yard, who corrupted the morals of a vast number of Canadian citizens, are multi-millionaires, controlling Canadian Distillers, one of the richest groups of people in this country. The making of that fortune, originated in a Regina junk yard, brought about the demoralization of many people both in the province in which I live and across the line in the United States, where they ran liquor successfully for years in violation of every law and every decency. It makes me shudder when I sometimes see those people in honoured places in this country-even sitting at the table of the king and queen when they came to Canada some time ago.
The only way to handle this business is to take it out of the hands of these people. They corrupt everything they touch. I do not speak as a fanatical teetotaller; for I was brought up in a home where we were taught to use liquor moderately, and I have never abused it, perhaps because of my early training. But if a provincial government stands in the way, that provincial government should be exposed and denounced. I think I know one provincial government which will stand in -the way, and I will name it: the government of Ontario, under the leadership of the present premier of this province, whose associations with the liquor business are pretty well known all across this country. The time has come when we ought to take a stand as a dominion parliament and say to these people: We are taking these young men into the armed forces; we are sending them here, there and everywhere, away from home, and as a dominion parliament and a dominion government we are going to see that these boys are properly protected against the traffic of people who have piled up huge fortunes out of this business.

I regret the minister has taken the attitude that because there is a dual jurisdiction, this government should not take any action and has no responsibility. I do not think that position will be satisfactory to the people of Canada. The responsibility of conducting this war is upon this government, not upon the provincial

Customs Tariff
governments. Of course I agree that the provincial governments, in their jurisdiction and within their spheres of influence, have a responsibility too in connection with the conduct of the war, but it is a relatively small responsibility as compared with that of the federal government. If this be a great evil, as is suggested and as I personally believe it to be, I do not think it is good enough for this government to take the attitude which has been indicated by the Minister of Finance, that it can do nothing because the crown in the right of the province has a sovereign jurisdiction coextensive. Actually, that jurisdiction is not quite co-extensive because it has nothing to do with the importation. I imagine the minister has not even had time to take up the matter with his colleagues since Monday last, but I suggest to him that public opinion will continue to press for some action by the dominion government. My suggestion was that a conference be called with these gentlemen with a view to arriving at an amicable arrangement whereby, through mutual action, an accommodation could be reached which would have the effect of reducing the retail sales. At the same time the federal government, within the sphere of its jurisdiction, could make some arrangement whereby importations also would be reduced, as well as the domestic manufacture, which are matters solely within the jurisdiction of the federal authority. This would release materials and labour for other and better purposes.
I am not advocating prohibition in war time. We had it once. I was very hopeful that it would succeed, and I must say that it was a great disappointment to me when it did not succeed. I place my support of prohibition not on ethical but on economic grounds. I saw how it operated in my own city for two years, and I must say that operation was effective. It can be done, but only if you have behind it two factors: first, a fearless enforcement of the law, which is sometimes difficult to obtain; and, second, a preponderance of public opinion in support of it.

To those who seek reformation along this line I say that before we can do away with one custom we have to replace it with something better, and I would like to ask hon. members what they have offered the minister as a substitute for the drinking that is taking place all over this country.
More milk.

If a custom is bad, we should replace it with a better custom, and I think there is a better one. You must change the thinking of those who practice that bad custom. If a boy is bad, or if there is a group
of boys meeting in a shack in the back lot, you can overcome the difficulty by keeping those boys busy doing something they will enjoy, something the motive behind which they may not understand. I am convinced that if we are to help in any reformation along these lines we must offer something better in its place, and I think that the senior Protestant chaplain, Bishop Wells, an old college friend of mine, has that. The only cure is for a man's thinking to be changed and for him to become a Christian through and through. That is the only cure for any evil habit.

There is one part of the minister's statement of a few moments ago which should not be allowed to pass without remark, and that was his reference to the provincial governments. The actual fact is that if this matter is left to the provincial governments nothing will be done. That is how it will work out, and the minister, if he will think it over, will come to the same conclusion. You have nine different governments -one province I believe has prohibition- and the urge is different in the different provinces, with different suggestions being made to the different governments. They are not under the same pressure of public opinion as we are here in Ottawa. The public, I am sure, are looking to the government of the nation to take the lead in this matter, because it is a national question .at this time. Money is being spent on liquor which should be diverted to the purchase of war savings certificates and war bonds. Men are being employed in the liquor industry who could be employed in war industry. Materials are being used in the liquor industry which could be used in manufacturing war equipment. Then, of course, there is the moral side of the question, and that is of the greatest importance, particularly in war time, when we have to get the right spirit instilled into the people of this country or Canada will not play her part in winning the war. There is a responsibility there which cannot be evaded by the dominion government or by this House of Commons. I do urge upon the minister again, as I did on Monday last, that he make a national appeal to the people, that he put the story before them with the authority of the Canadian government behind the appeal. I think the results would be surprisingly effective. I urge upon him that he take action right away along that line.

I wish to support the suggestion which was made by the leader of the opposition. If the government is unwilling to do anything more it should at least institute a programme of education across the
Customs Tariff

country. Certainly more leadership would be given to the provinces if a convention or conference were called at which this question could be threshed out and a solution found that would be Acceptable to the provinces and the dominion. This government owes it to the Canadian people to show at least that degree of leadership in this time of national crisis.

I would ask the minister a question arising out of a statement by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The attitude taken by the minister is that this is a provincial matter, while, in point of fact, having regard to the size of the problem and its effect upon the war effort in general, it is a great national problem. The distribution of intoxicating liquors is a matter for the provinces ; but have the provinces been approached by the dominion government with a view to securing their cooperation in a campaign to reduce the sale and consumption of liquor? If so, what has been the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have discussed the matter with representatives of more than one province, but in no formal way have we told the provinces what we thought their duty was.
Did they tell you?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, and they do not often tell us what our duty is.
Sometimes they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am temperamentally averse to telling people what their duty is or telling governments what their duty is. The likely answer would be that they are pretty well informed as to what their duty is, that they know the situation. I was thinking when members were speaking that there is nothing to prevent any member from holding meetings in his constituency and asking the people to drink less.
The suggestion is that the government of Canada should advise the people on their personal habits, thereby assisting the churches and other persons whose duty it is to do that. The reason why the dominion government is being urged to do this is that a change in these particular habits would assist in the war effort. There are a great many other habits of the Canadian people that could be changed to the advantage of the war effort. I suppose there is no reason why the dominion government should not point this out from time to time, but the idea of bringing together the provincial governments and telling them, "Here, do better than you are doing," is a suggestion that would not :be welcomed by some governments, particularly by those who

are doing their level best to curb this evil. I am speaking about the government of Nova Scotia. I know how they have struggled, and the curtailment there, so far as I can see, has not amounted to anything at all. The people have the money, they want the liquor, and they are buying it. Surely the provincial governments, faced with these very local situations that were mentioned this afternoon, are in a better position to deal with them than is the dominion government. I would far rather see people spend their money on war savings certificates or bonds than in buying liquor.
Why not tell them so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have told them that. I have told them for the last one or two years to curtail their expenditures.
And the people have been doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some have and some have not. I have probably met with some success, but not by any means with spectacular success, in view of purchases from the liquor stores being about 50 per cent higher than they were the year before the war, despite all our talk about sacrifice. I am just pointing out that it is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say, "Mr. Dominion Government, you are the one to make people drink less liquor"; but it is not as simple as that.

The onus is on the dominion government to solve this problem. The government of the day cannot treat this simply as a question of prohibition or temperance or a question of morals; it is a war question. The government are approaching it wholly from the point of view of revenue. They have practically abolished provincial and municipal institutions as they have existed under the British North America Act. I should like to have the attention of the hon. member for Moose Jaw and of other members of the committee, who should be interested in what is being said. The fathers of confederation saw fit to design and carve out provinces and municipalities, which were given certain legislative powers under the British North America Act. They were given certain powers with respect to taxation. The government cannot shelter itself behind the idea that this is a provincial and not a federal matter; it is entirely a war problem. Secondly, the municipalities were obliged under the constitution to provide police protection and other necessary services.
They had a reduction of licences campaign many times. The province took the revenues, and all the municipalities had to say about

Customs Tariff
it was that the owner and the property should be satisfactory in order to get a licence.
I have never been in a new beer parlour since they have been allowed in the province I live in, although I am not by any means a temperance man or prohibitionist. I look for some sanity from the government on this question. During the last war soldiers were placed in camps which were located a long way from any form of transportation; they put up with untold hardships. Soldiers need stimulants in their canteens. This is known by most of the military men, and they feel that nothing should be done to legislate against soldiers in canteens. When I was head of the city and chairman of the police commission of Toronto riots broke out near the close of the last wrar about foreigners and licences. Foreign people who had only recently come to the country were holding most of the licences for restaurants and other places. While prohibition was on in Ontario, civilians were able to stock their cellars with wet goods of all kinds, and when the soldiers came home they found prohibition in effect and bootlegging going on. When the troops returned they could' buy nothing. When we had prohibition in Ontario and other provinces; it was simply an incentive for the bootlegger to flourish like a green bay tree, which he did. The law was not a success.	[DOT]
I have received a good many resolutions regarding this question. If there is one thing that will drive a>
man to drink, it is the budget of the Minister of Finance. In my opinion, it is acting both as hangman and undertaker for the small retailer and wholesaler alike. Never mind what a whole battalion of hired press experts paid by the government say of the budget. It is confiscation to the small property owner and worker.
As to beer, according to bank statements and returns made by various departments many distillers and brewers were making a lot of money-the brewers especially-and were taxed little. We are compared with the United States. The brewers are violating the law on billboard advertising and pages in papers, and they will violate this new clause of the tariff also. At the present time they advertise on billboards throughout the country and attempt to capitalize on the man in the navy, the army and the air force. In my opinion wisdom and leadership in arriving at a solution of this question is lacking. Full control over this matter has been placed in the hands of the minister and his department by the War Measures Act.
The government of Canada has the responsibility to take up this question because of the changed conditions brought about by the war and the fact that the enemy is at both our front and back doors. They have failed in this responsibility. The onus of solving this question is not on this committee, it is on the government of the day as long as they are the government. They should be able to arrive at a sane and reasonable settlement of this question, especially in war time. Because of this budget the price of milk in the canteens has been put up to six cents, and beer, cigarettes, ice cream, sandwiches, coffee, tea and other liquids have gone up a cent or two. The minister should make a national survey and study the policy and come to a decision. He should know what they are doing in Great Britain and by our allies and the other dominions; and also the civil side of it should be gone into.
The minister is always preaching against luxuries; here is a good chance to practice it. There was considerable criticism in a Toronto weekly paper about the amount of money the minister's own department spent in connection with the victory loan and the war savings campaign-cigars, hotel expenses, banquets and refreshments. There has been no statement from the department contradicting what was said about this extravagence or stating their policy. As I say, the onus is on the government to solve this question, to provide a fair, reasonable and just settlement for all classes of the community. The soldier should not be lost sight of and his privileges should not be taken away without his consent.
When in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier the clergy came to ask him for prohibition and a vote, the chairman of the delegation, Rev. Mr. Huxtable, found Sir Wilfrid most democratic. In the days of Sir Oliver Mowat and Mr. Ross every licensed victualler had to be a Liberal and help to raise a campaign fund. When Sir James Whitney came into power he introduced wise temperance legislation and the three-fifths clause and aided temperance. It was a sensible law and provided proper control.
The onus is not only on the minister; it rests also upon the other members of the government. There are some from Ontario but we do not see much of them. Ontario is the forgotten province in connection with confederation. The four cabinet ministers from Ontario-Toronto has none-should give heed to the people of that province on this question and aid in a solution. There is no doubt at all that much money is being

wasted. The minister is asking everybody to save, but we should be able to read the handwriting for war reform on the wall. As I say, I believe the onus is on the government and they should solve this question.

Who is responsible for the runners or agents of the breweries and distilleries? Every session since 1940 I have had men come to my room in the hotel and ask if Mr. So-and-So was in. When I replied, "no," they would say that they wanted to sell him a case of such and such a brand of beer and wondered if I did not want a case. The same thing with liquor. They would intimate they had an order from this fictitious man and then try to sell me a few bottles. That sort of practice is to encourage people to buy. I do not know who is responsible, but these men are going around the hotels. I have had this happen here as well as in Toronto and Hamilton, although I have not bought any yet.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide:-

A. Rates of tax applicable to persons other than corporations and joint stock companies:-
I. Normal tax-

(a)	a married person,
(b)	a widow or widower with a son or daughter under eighteen years of age and wholly dependent upon such taxpayer for support, or a son or daughter eighteen years of age or over and dependent on account of mental or physical infirmity, or a son or daughter under twenty-one years of age who is dependent upon such parent for support on proof that such child is a student at secondary school, university, or other educational institution;
(c)	an individual other than a married person, who maintains a self-contained domestic establishment and who actually supports therein a person wholly dependent upon him and connected with him by blood relationship, marriage or adoption;
