When the budget was under consideration a short time ago, I took occasion to analyse the proposals of the minister in considerable detail. I do not propose to cover the same ground again in the committee stage, but I would recall to his mind that with respect to various matters I asked that careful consideration be given to the representations which I made. I hope that as we reach the appropriate resolution he will indicate his response to the suggestions I then made. '
Coming now to the specific proposals in the resolution 1, I desire to make a few observations.
I think the minister should explain directly and first of all why he did not go the whole distance in consolidating the old national defence tax, which is to expire on August 31 of this year, and the graduated income tax, into a single assessment. No doubt the reason is that the old national defence tax and its successor, the new normal tax, differ in some degree, at least, in principle from the graduated income tax, in that they are assessable against the total income of any person whose income exceeds a specified amount. I think we do not have to go very far afield to seek the reason. Because of the non-consolidation of these two taxes, the minister is enabled to strike more heavily at the lower income tax groups. That, I think, is the objective, the very skilfully concealed objective of the major part of this budget. The minister is striking the heaviest blow at recipients of small incomes that this nation has ever witnessed, and in doing so he has, and I think by design, put a crippling tax on a class of our people who will find the very greatest difficulty in meeting the imposition. In that regard there has been gross discrimination, and especially is that true, as I shall point out at a later stage, and as I have already pointed out in the remarks I made on the budget some days ago, between married men in the smaller income tax groups and single men in the same groups.
. I would have thought that to combine the two taxes would have led to much greater simplicity for the tax-collecting officials of the Department of National Revenue, and certainly for the individual taxpayer. That is a criticism which I make of the proposals of the minister. Does the minister think it would not have been possible to combine the two taxes, to refrain from bearing so heavily upon a low income tax group, and to achieve a more simplified and logical tax structure? That is the summation of what I have said heretofore, divided into three parts.
I believe that the two taxes should have been combined, that he should have refrained from bearing so heavily upon the lower income tax groups, and should have achieved a more simplified and logical tax structure.
The second point in connection with the normal tax to which I desire to refer is that the proposed rates indicate an apparent and, I believe, a very real discrimination between married and single persons. That is in connection now with the normal tax, because we must bear in mind that there are two taxes, the normal tax and the graduated income
Income War Tax Act

tax. I assert that there is not only an apparent but a real discrimination with respect to the normal tax as between married and single persons. The rate of tax on married persons is 7 per cent if the income exceeds $1,200 per annum. In the case of a single person it is 7 per cent if the income exceeds $660 but does not exceed $1,800. Between $1,800 and $3,000 the tax is 8 per cent, and over $3,000 it is 9 per cent. Consequently, hon. gentlemen will see that in the bracket between $1,200 and $1,800 the normal tax of a married person and the normal tax of a single person are identical.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In what range is that?

Between $1,200 and $1,800. At least that is my conclusion and, if I am incorrect, I shall be delighted to have the error pointed out. I do not think the minister will contend that this is fair and equitable. Surely a married person in the low income status should be given on the normal tax rate greater consideration than the single person. That is a principle for which I shall contend, and for which I shall invite the cooperation of members on all sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
referring only to the normal tax.
Yes; I laid emphasis on that. The point I raise is in connection with the normal tax alone. I am coming to the other; it is bad enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have to take both to-get the results.	[DOT]

You have to take them together to get the real tax bill for the two, but I am trying to analyse this and I hope I am doing so fairly and accurately. I will take the responsibility for doing so fairly; I hope I am accurate and I think I am. I suggest that the married person in the low income status should be given on this normal tax rate greater consideration than the single person, and I shall carry the judgment of the house and the country with me in that proposition. If there is any income status in which the married person should be given consideration, I suggest that it is certainly in this very low status-the married man getting between $1,200 and $1,800. In the larger communities, in the big cities, a salary of between $1,200 and $1,800 is not considered a large salary; but in the smaller communities, in the large towns and small cities, we have no big salaries at all. There is no one, with possibly one exception, in my town with a salary in excess of $15,000 [Mr It. B. Hanson.]
a year. On the average the salaries are low. Take the' salaries paid by the provincial government of New Brunswick. They are and always have been meagre; and if you leave out the salaries of judges, which are statutory and paid by this dominion, and look at the salaries of the rank and file of our citizens, occupying various positions, men of good standing in the community, you will find a large number of them who get only between $1,200 and $1,800. But they are the men in the community who support the churches. They are the men who support community effort. They are the men in the community, none of them with large salaries, who are called upon to do jobs through the Rotary club and the other service clubs. They are married men, with children whom they are endeavouring to bring up to be the backbone of the future citizenship of the country. They are the people who have to struggle, even in normal times, to give their children education and to provide life insurance, and who usually die leaving behind them very little but a good name-the most worthy class of citizens we have.
The salt of the earth.

They are the salt of the earth. I could name many of them in my own community who will be terribly hard hit by this budget. These are men who are doing what they can t< comply with the appeal of the minister to buy war savings certificates. They have authorized their employers to deduct regularly from their pay envelopes their contributions to the national effort. Then there is the group of men in my community-I mention this class because it illustrates a large proportion of the whole field throughout the country-comprising the artisans. The artisan in good times makes from $100 to $150 a month. He is in the same category as the salaried class, and in my part of the country he is a grand citizen. He is the man who takes an interest and has always been represented in the city council, who makes his contribution to the community, and he is in exactly the same position as the salaried man. These people are being terribly penalized by this budget. Then there is the bachelor, who has no family responsibility at all. I venture to suggest that if you analyse the position of the family man with a wife and two children, as compared with the position of the bachelor, you will find that the family man is given a total advantage of only $400 per annum as against the bachelor, the young unmarried man in the same income tax bracket.
That is a gross discrimination. These ' bachelors are spenders. The married man

Income War Tax Act
spends his money, to be sure, but necessity requires him to do so. He spends it on necessities for the support of his family, in bringing up the future generation, whereas many of the other class fritter away their income on useless expenditures. I make a plea for better treatment of the married man in the income tax groups that I have indicated, as opposed to the other citizens. I hope that is one feature of the budget which the minister will reconsider.
Still dealing with the normal tax-I will confine what I have to say to this resolution 1-so far as deductions from the normal tax are concerned, I suggest to the minister that the allowance of $28 for each child or dependent is very small.
Too small.
Chicken feed.

If I
appreciate the minister's position, it is based on the capitalized value of the previous exemption. I do not know how he figures it out. I recall many a debate in this house in days gone by, from 1921 on, in which pleas were made by members for greater consideration to heads of families in respect of exemptions for children and especially to those men who had large families. I remember a most eloquent plea made by an hon. gentleman who now graces the superior court bench of the province of Quebec, Mr. Justice Archambault. I remember having joined with him in his request to a former minister of finance in that regard, and our having convinced the minister of finance of that day of the justice of our plea for consideration for the family man, especially the man with the large family.
There was an old, trite saying that two people could live as cheaply as one, but I found the fallacy of that saying very shortly after I got married. I think we will all agree that it is a fallacy. You cannot do it, especially under modern conditions. I am making [DOT]a plea on behalf of the family man, especially the family man with a small income. I know what the struggle is. I have gone through it myself, trying to live and keep up a position and be a useful member of the community on a small income. So I appeal to the minister to reconsider the schedules in so far as they affect the men of small income. I especially appeal now for more credit than $28 a year being given for each dependent child. I realize that that is $28 off the tax. But I suggest to the minister that it should be more. I will say this in justice to the minister-I want to be fair in my remarks-that the allowance of $28 per
annum for each child or dependent is an increase over the allowance made under the national defence tax during the last two years, and for that I give the minister that much thanks.
The deduction to be allowed under paragraph (iii) of subsection 2 of resolution 1 perpetuates an anomaly and an inequality with respect to guest children against which we have protested for the past two years. Only to-day I had a long distance telephone call from a man in this province who felt the injustice of that. I submit that to limit that deduction to the case of children brought from the United Kingdom under a government-sponsored plan, and to deny it to those brought to Canada voluntarily or under an unsponsored plan, is a discrimination that should be done away with. I know it will be said at once that many of these children are the children of the rich. That, however, is not universally true. I could show you in my city three lovely English boys whose father occupies just a moderate position in an insurance company in the city of London.
I had the pleasure of visiting him when over there in order that I might report to him as to the physical well-being of his three boys. Those boys were taken into a good home in Fredericton. The head of that family neither has received nor expects to receive any recompense-although he probably will, I think, receive it when conditions arise making it possible-not only for the cash outlay. Not one cent is being allowed him on his income tax for having taken those children in and perhaps having preserved their lives, because I understand their home on the Thames has been bombed out-fortunately the family had moved-while someone else who brought two or three children out under a government plan is given some consideration.
This is not a plea for the rich man whose children are taken in. Many of the children brought out here were brought just out of the good-will of those who wanted to see them survive. I regret that further use was not made of the plan or system. We should have brought out many more British children to Canadian homes. I think this should have been done by the government itself, but I am not going to find fault with the government because I do not know all the circumstances. The reason given was scarcity of transportation, and that may be an adequate reason; no doubt there are others. An hon. member suggests there was perhaps discrimination in England. I do not know enough about that to discuss it. I realize that it was not possible to take all the children. Many of the children of the poor
Income War Tax Act

did not want to come anyway, did not want to be separated from their families. I confine my criticism to the rigid attitude of the government in not giving more consideration to the question of exemption on account of these children. I would urge the minister to reconsider that position.
Subsection 3 of resolution 1 carries forward the principle of the national defence tax, that the tax shall not be permitted to reduce the income below $660 and $1,200 respectively. This brings to my attention one of the anomalies of our tax structure as it exists in this budget. A married man in receipt of $1,200 annually pays no tax. A married man in receipt of $1,250 pays $50 tax. A married man in receipt of $1,300 pays $100 tax. The result is that the tax reduces the income of a wage-earner or a salaried man receiving $1,300 to the same level as the man receiving 81,200. While it is true that one-half of the tax payable is the minimum savings requirement, eventually refundable to the taxpayer, it does seem to me an anomaly that a man drawing $1,300 actually receives no more than a man with an income of $1,200. I shall stop there. That is just the first instalment.

I rise to urge the minister to grant further exemption to officers of the armed forces who are not now receiving exemption. Under the present law, as I understand it, warrant officers, noncommissioned officers and men of the active service forces-that is, other ranks-are exempt from income tax. That is as it ought to be;
I have no quarrel with that. Commissioned officers while on active service beyond Canada are also exempt from the payment of income tax, and that is as it should be. On the other hand, commissioned officers who have volunteered for service, who have been found to be within the required medical category and have been accepted, must pay income tax so long as they are serving in Canada. Exemption should be granted to these men as well. They are holding themselves ready and willing for active service anywhere in the world, and they should not have to pay this tax. At the present time, if we take the tax into consideration, the pay of a warrant officer is higher than that of a lieutenant.

Higher
than that of a major, is it not?

The pay of a warrant officer is higher than that of a captain and, as I figure it, equal to that of a major.
I am not taking any objection to the pay of the warrant officer; he is not paid too much. Nor am I belittling his responsibilities, for they are considerable. But I think it must [Mr }{. B. Hanson.]
be admitted that the lieutenant, the captain and the major all have much more responsibility than the warrant officer has, yet under the present set-up their pay is less. The non-commissioned officers, warrant officers and other ranks do not have to pay a cent for clothing or equipment. Commissioned officers have to pay for nearly all their clothing and personal equipment. I submit that this is not right, and I hope the minister will see the injustice and unfairness of it and take the necessary steps to have it corrected.
I should like to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary East.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out that military exemptions hardly come within the scope of this resolution. I have been reading the resolutions in an attempt to see where the subject being discussed could be brought up, but I do not see how it can be done.

May I point out that the question has arisen and has become of importance because of the great increase in the rate of income tax. Of course that comes under the first paragraph of this resolution, and I submit that this is the only paragraph under which that subject can be discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I may interrupt for a moment, I intend to present to the committee a recommendation in regard to this matter, by way of an amendment.
To what section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be an additional resolution, I think, and perhaps the matter can be discussed at that stage. It is not to the effect that the hon. member for Calgary East has recommended, but it will deal with the matter.
Could we have it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it is not ready. It is one of those things on which I am working.
. Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): Is there any section under which a discussion of the topic raised by the hon. member for Calgary East would be relevant or pertinent, if it is not resolution 1? I think we ought to do this in as orderly a manner as possible, with a view to getting through quickly. If we jump from one thing to another we are not likely to get through so quickly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that there is any resolution here that would cover it.

He has to have a chance to make his statement somewhere.

Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite agree; and if for any reason I should say the government does not propose to do anything about the matter, I will undertake that it can be discussed on some resolution before we finish, but I expect that a resolution will be added dealing with the matter.

The minister has intimated that he proposes to bring in an amendment. It might be helpful to him in drawing up the amendment if we were permitted to make our statements at this stage instead of waiting until the amendment is brought down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My difficulty is that I
have allowed the hon. member for Calgary East to make a statement, and I should not like to preclude the hon. member for Vancouver South from the same opportunity, because I want to mete out the same treatment to all hon. members. So, if the hon. gentleman has a few remarks to offer on the subject, I will permit him to do so.

The question has been well
covered by the hon. member for Calgary East, but there are one or two other aspects to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister and the committee. These officers are taxed not only on their pay but also on the allowances paid for their wives and children, and in addition, I believe, they are taxed on their rations, calculated at the rate of SI a day. In other words, for taxation purposes the sum of $365 is added to their pay. With regard to the dependents' allowance, when this is taxed it means that the allowance is paid out with one hand and taken back with the other.
This taxation also hits officers who come back from overseas. Many officers have been brought back this year to train the troops in Canada, and I understand that the moment they arrive in Canada they become subject to income tax, .whereas while overseas they were not. It affects the men who come up from the ranks. The policy of the government has been to bring up officers from the ranks. I think that is a sound policy. But if this taxation is to apply to those men who take commissions, looking at it from the monetary point of view a man might be foolish to accept a commission; he might be far wiser to remain in the ranks. After all, we have now only the one army. The men on the Pacific coast may be in action before the men in Great Britain, and it does seem unfair that there should be this distinction. These men are the leaders of the army. I believe they feel that this taxation is most unfair; the fact that it is imposed upon them is causing great uneasiness, and that is bound, in the
long run, to affect the army. Looking at the question from the point of view of the defence of Canada and the need to have an efficient army here, I submit to the minister that this tax should be removed.
Then I would point out that at the present time the exemption does not cover merchant seamen, civilian firemen who have gone overseas, or men in the auxiliary services. Men in these groups should be included among those exempt from the payment of income tax. I do not think anyone in this house would suggest for a moment that the merchant seamen are not deserving of the utmost consideration, yet they do not get the benefit of this exemption. I would urge that the minister keep these facts in mind when he is drafting his amendments, so that all the officers in the army may be granted exemption as well as the men in the merchant service, the firemen serving overseas and the men in the auxiliary services.

And
the women.

I should like to support the remarks made by the two previous speakers. I think this is very unfair legislation, especially to those officers who have been overseas andi have been brought back to this country for instructional purposes, and I hope that the minister in drafting the amendments will give this class due consideration.
I should like to endorse the remarks made by my leader. As I pointed out when speaking on another matter yesterday, while I have great sympathy for the minister in his gigantic undertaking, if he is not very careful he will find that this budget will be termed the home-wreckers' budget, and that applies most directly to the personal income tax provisions. One would think that a set of bachelors and bankers had drawn up this budget for the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why bankers?

The moneyed interests are taken care of to a certain extent, and certainly this budget does discriminate against the family man. It is much easier for the bachelor to maintain himself and get along than it is for the man with a large family, and I w'ould not give very much for the future of our nation if we had to depend entirely on the bachelors.
I consider the $80 deduction which the taxpayer can make from his >x as an exemption for a child, instead of being allowed the old $400 exemption, is another direct blow at the family man because it
Income War Tax Act

makes certain that he comes within the higher brackets. Many a family man with a fairly large family will find it almost impossible to raise his family properly and continue as a good citizen of the community. The budget is discriminative in that respect.
With reference to the compulsory savings feature, I do not know whether it is intended that an employee must give his employer a detailed statement of his personal financial affairs, stating what life insurance premiums he is paying, how much principal on a mortgage and matters of that kind, so that the proper deduction may be made. But if that is the intention, I consider it very improper. Employees should not be called upon to lay bare all their private affairs before their employers. It is not clear whether that is required by the legislation.
Further, if. a man is buying his home under an agreement of sale, he should be allowed to make a deduction just as if he were buying his home under the mortgage plan. The resolution states nothing about that, although the man who is purchasing his home under an agreement of sale is to all intents and purposes under exactly the same financial set-up as a man with a mortgage on his home, and should be given the same consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree.

Thank you. I trust
that the minister will give serious thought to the position of the average family man and that he will make the necessary adjustments. The budget works a distinct hardship on the family man, the greatest asset that any nation can have. We shall not have much of a future if we do not encourage and look after the family man. *

I wish to speak on behalf of the men who are taking the officers' training course in the two training centres in Canada, one at Brockville and the other at Gordon Head. I have been most reliably informed that since the introduction of this new schedule of taxes for officers the applications for taking the course have materially decreased in number. In other words, the men who now hold the rank of warrant officer do not wish to be promoted. I have heard it argued: "Surely these men must have some ambition and must want to be promoted from non-commissioned officer to commissioned officer." But I come back to the argument that was made by the minister himself last night, when he spoke of the necessity for some incentive. The incentive in this particular case must be that an officer should receive a little something more than he was getting as

a non-commissioned officer, because when he assumes the rank of commissioned officer he immediately assumes greater responsibilities. I am afraid that if the officers who have been returned from England and are destined to remain in Canada are required to pay income taxation under the present schedules, we are going to have a dearth of officers in the Canadian army.
The leader of the opposition has referred to refugee children who were not brought out under a government-sponsored scheme. In Brockville there is a boys' school which, for S400 a year, has been looking after, educating and feeding refugee children, and in some instances actually clothing them. The headmaster of the school told me the other day that the sponsors of no less than three children at the school had notified him that they could no longer continue to keep the children at the school because they were unable to pay for their board and keep.
I have also in mind a school that was opened in Toronto for refugee children who were brought over, not under any government-sponsored scheme, but under a private scheme. The children are placed among various families, and no distinction is made between rich and poor so long as the child gets a good home. That school had at one time between thirty and forty children, but to-day it is closed because the children have all been placed. Those children cost those who have undertaken to look after them just as much as it would cost to look after a child brought out under a government-sponsored scheme, and I plead with the minister to provide the same exemption in both instances. The people who have taken those children into their homes have done so out of the bigness of their hearts, and should receive equal consideration with those who are looking after children brought out under government-sponsored schemes.	[DOT]

I was very much interested in the remark made by the leader of the opposition with respect to exemptions for children. Being of an inquisitive mind I looked up the records to see how these exemptions would affect the members of the House of Commons, and I find that one member has thirteen children, two have eleven and two have nine. None of these hon. gentlemen has risen in his seat to protest against the exemptions for children as provided under this budget.
So far as exemptions for men in the armed forces are concerned, I trust that the minister will take cognizance of the powerful arguments that have been put forward this afternoon with respect to officers of units which

Income War Tax Act
are not overseas. No doubt some errors will be made in connection with this income tax, but I know they will not be by design. But if they are made, I think they should be made in favour of the man who is on active service rather than in favour of the civilian. It might be all very well as a technical argument to say that if a man is serving in the armed forces in Canada he is perhaps a brass hat at headquarters who woidd enjoy this exemption from income tax, but there is more to it than that. Over the week-end I took the opportunity to talk with a number of officers who are on active service in Canada, and I may tell the minister that their voices on this matter were pretty vigorous. One officer told me that it was the subject of acrimonious conversation in practically every mess in Canada. These increased income taxes have placed officers in Canadian units in a position in which they feel they are actually the object of discrimination. I said to one officer that no doubt the government had in mind the fact that some men would never see overseas service, that while they wore the king's uniform they were actually occupying semi-civilian positions. He said that that might be true in an odd instance, but he did not see why the government should discriminate against those who were not in that category. He said there might be only one out of a hundred to whom that could apply. He argued, and I agree with him, that men who have volunteered for active service anywhere should be granted similar exemptions to those granted to others in the service.
I think it will be found that this new tax structure will interfere to no small degree with the morale of our armed forces in Canada. It must be remembered that it is not an easy thing for some of these men to stay here and wait long months for the order to proceed overseas and for some action to occur. It is also not easy for them to see some of their neighbours and their friends in civilian life making greater earnings than they are. In many instances they have been stopped in their tracks, economically and financially speaking, and they are not feeling any too happy over the comparisons they can make. It seems to me that the government might grant these men the same exemption that is granted to others in the armed forces, for the purposes of morale if for no other reason. I am fortified in my argument by comments which have been made in the press from time to time, and I should like to refer particularly to an item which appeared
in the Toronto Daily Star of June 30. One sentence has particular reference to the subject under debate. It reads:
Among the "new poor" emerging from the smoke and fumes of the recent budget blast at Ottawa, will be commissioned officers, men who have "gone active" but who have been kept on duty in Canada by order of the higher command.
Then at the end the article quotes some figures. I have not checked them, but I think they are fairly accurate. I quote:
As against this a warrant officer (class A), with trade pay and a separation allowance for his wife of $40 a month would have a net income of $2,306.75. A promotion for him would be a financial set-back unless he jumped all the way to the rank of major.
This is not a fair way to treat men, whether they are overseas or in Canada. I make a last minute appeal to the minister to reconsider and review the whole position of officers in Canadian units.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to suggest an amendment as follows:
That part I of resolution 1 and resolution 3 be amended by adding the following words to each:
"Provided that in the case of a wife who is in receipt of earned income in excess of $660 per year, the wife may be treated as a single taxpayer and the husband may be treated as a married taxpayer for income tax purposes."

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I move accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By way of explanation I may say that we are informed that quite a substantial number of married women are proposing to leave employment because it will pay them to do so as a result of these income tax schedules. This amendment may prove a considerable cost to the treasury, but I am afraid we shall have to make it in order to prevent this exodus from employment. This will be the only amendment to part I.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock. Progress reported.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM COLONEL DREW-OPINION OF GOVERNMENT COUNSEL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM COLONEL DREW-OPINION OF GOVERNMENT COUNSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the house to return to motions, to permit me to make a brief statement.
Hong Kong Commission

The house having reverted to the order for motions:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTER FROM COLONEL DREW-OPINION OF GOVERNMENT COUNSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, in replying to the request of my hon. friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) for a copy of a letter addressed to me by Colonel Drew, I said to my hon. friend that if he would take the responsibility of asking that the letter be tabled, it would be tabled. Subsequently I felt that, having regard to the contents of the letter and having regard to the inquiry to which it referred and the nature of the inquiry, I had better obtain legal opinion in the first instance as to whether it would be proper for me in any case to table the letter. I accordingly, through the Department of Justice, secured an opinion from Mr. George A. Campbell, K.C., who was counsel for the government in the Hong Kong inquiry, and I should like to read to my hon. friend and to the house the opinion which Mr. Campbell has given me.
The communication is as follows:
Ottawa, July 15, 1942. Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King,

Prime Minister of Canada,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Hear Prime Minister,
re: Hong Kong inquiry I have just had an opportunity of reading the communication dated July 11, 1942, addressed to you by Mr. George A. Drew, K.C.,. who acted as counsel nominated by the Hon. Mr. Hanson, K.C., during the recent Hong Kong inquiry and I have considered the question submitted as to whether or not it would be proper for you to table that communication before the House of Commons.
This document purports to disclose a very considerable number of facts and to refer to the contents of several documents said to have been put in evidence before the commissioner during the recent inquiry. For reasons hereinafter stated, I am not free to discuss the accuracy or inaccuracy of any such references.
At the outset of the inquiry an order in council, P.C. 1039, was passed on March 2, 1942, which had the effect of clothing the commissioner in this and any other investigation concerning the armed forces of Canada with all the powers and authority of a judge of any superior court in Canada while exercising his judicial functions, including specifically the power and authority of making and enforcing any order made by him concerning any inquiry held in camera in order to safeguard the secrecy of such inquiry.
In the exercise of that authority, Sir Hyman P. Duff, Chief Justice of Canada, who sat as commissioner in the Hong Kong inquiry, ruled and directed that the inquiry before him should be held in camera and it was held in camera. In my opinion, all counsel who participated in the inquiry were bound by, and by their 
continued presence, acquiesced in that ruling. It flows from such ruling that all persons,
including counsel were specifically enjoined as to their duty to preserve secrecy as to testimony given, documents produced and all other evidence placed before the commissioner, and that order directed all persons not knowingly to infringe upon such secrecy.
At the conclusion of the hearing for the taking of testimony in this matter, and some days before the date fixed for completion of the hearing of oral argument, all counsel concerned received notice from the commissioner requiring them on the day of the final hearing of oral argument to deliver up to the secretary of the commission any and all transcripts of evidence, exhibits and copies thereof, written arguments and copies thereof, notes of evidence and any and all other writings and documents relating in any way whatsoever to the matters in question.
It appears from page 32 of Mr. Drew's communication that it purports largely to be based upon his written argument to the commissioner, of which presumably therefore he retained a copy in his possession. In his letter he gives a number of verbatim quotations from the transcript of evidence and exhibits.
Mr. Drew's letter purports to give the effect of a number of confidential communications received by the government of Canada from the government of the United Kingdom, the disclosure of which was only consented to by the government of the United Kingdom subject to a specific condition that the disclosure was to be limited to the commissioner and counsel only, and solely for the purpose of the inquiry; and the commissioner was not permitted to reproduce these communications in his report. [DOT]Any disclosure, therefore, even to the House of Commons, would in my opinion be a violation of the substance of that condition, i Jf' therefore, Mr. Drew's communication is tabled by you before the House of Commons I am of the opinion that you will be violating a condition under which the government of the United Kingdom consented to the disclosure to the commissioner and counsel of those telegrams.
I am, moreover, of the opinion that Mr. Drew's communication purports to contain a considerable number of extracts from evidence and reference to exhibits which do not appear in the published report of the commissioner and th£ appendix to it. If, therefore, you should table the document you are, in my opinion, to that extent participating in and thereby condoning a violation of the order of secrecy with which the proceedings in camera were to be and were in fact conducted.
A ours faithfully,
Geo. A. Campbell.
I should, I think, place on record with this communication the copy of the order in council which is referred to in the early portion of it.
At the Government House at Ottawa Monday, the 2nd day of March, 1942.
His Excellency the Governor General in Council
Whereas the Prime Minister reports that, in his opinion, it is desirable that a commissioner conducting any inquiry under the Inquiries Act,

Hong Kong Commission
R.S.C., 1927, Ch. 99, involving investigation into any matter concerning the armed forces of Canada should have certain immunities and powers;
Now, therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, and under and by virtue of the powers vested in the governor in council by the War Measures Act, Ch. 206 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, is pleased to order and doth hereby order that, where under any order of the governor in council, heretofore or hereafter made, a commissioner is appointed under the Inquiries Act, Ch. 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, to enquire into any matter concerning the armed forces of Canada, such commissioner shall have all the immunities enjoyed by any judge of any superior court in Canada while exercising his judicial functions, and that any and all powers and authority of any such judge relating to any contempt of court, whether committed in the face of the court or elsewhere, shall be vested in such commissioner in respect of such inquiry; and in particular, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, that such commissioner shall have all the powers, jurisdiction and authority of any such judge for the purpose of enforcing any order made by him concerning any inquiry held in camera in order to safeguard the secrecy thereof.
A. D. P. Heeney,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
What are the dates of the order in council my right hon. friend has just read, and of the order in council authorizing the inquiry?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The date of this order in council is Monday, March 2, 1942. I have not the date of the other.
Well, that was made subsequently to the original. That is the second order in council, and I never heard of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will find that it was tabled with the other orders in council.
Then I should add the following communication, which relates to what I have just read; a communication from Mr. Campbell to the commissioner, the Chief Justice, written to-day:	.
Ottawa, July 15, 1942.
Right Honourable Sir Lyman P. Huff,

Chief Justice of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir Lyman:
Re-Hong Kong inquiry
May I, as counsel for the government of Canada, ask you who, as royal commissioner, conducted the Hong Kong inquiry that you permit the secretary of the commission to certify and hand to me for the use of the
Prime Minister a copy of the order which you verbally gave directing that the proceedings be held in camera?	_
If you approve, the secretary might also indicate that immediately preceding the making of that order you read order in council P.C. 1639, dated March 2, 1942.
Yours faithfully,
Geo. A. Campbell.
Then the letter from the commissioner, the chief justice, to Mr. Campbell, in reply:
15th July, 1942.
Dear Mr. Campbell:
Re-Hong Kong Inquiry I have your letter of to-day and as requested I have authorized Mr. W. Kenneth Campbell, the secretary of the commission, to hand you for the use of the Prime Minister, a copy of the order which I made regarding the holding of the inquiry in camera.
The secretary will also indicate that immediately preceding the making of my order I read the operative part of order in council, P.C. 1639, dated March 2, 1942.
Yours faithfully,

Geo. A. Campbell, Esq., K.C.,
Chateau Laurier,
Ottawa.
The enclosure with that letter is as follows: Ottawa, July 15, 1942.
Re Hong Kong inquiry I certify that at the session of the inquiry held on March 4, 1942, the commissioner read the operative part of order in council P.C. 1639, dated March 2, 1942, and made the following order:	-
"I think it desirable, also, to state formally for the purpose of the record that this inquiry has from the beginning been held in camera and is and will henceforth be held in camera. That imports, it is perhaps unnecessary to say, the duty on the part of everybody present to preserve secrecy as to the testimony given, documents produced, and all other evidence placed before the commission, as well as the duty on the part of all persons not knowingly to infringe upon such secrecy."
W. Kenneth Campbell,
Secretary to the Commission.
I have placed on Hansard the legal opinion that has been given to me. In the circumstances I hope my hon. friend will not expect me to table the communication, because I should feel that.it would not be proper for me to do so in my position as Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
With the indulgence of the
house, and, I think, as a matter of right, I desire to make a few observations. First of all, the inquiry itself should never have been held in camera and the original order in council did not so provide. The order in council dated March 2, which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has now
Hong Kong Commission

read, was never brought to my attention by anybody. The fact that such an order in council was passed by the government was kept a secret as well, and it should never have been passed, because this was intended to be a full public inquiry. That was the promise made in this house. It was not a full public inquiry.
After the inquiry was held and the report was brought down and tabled, I asked that the evidence be laid upon the table so that the members of the house and the public might be in a position to judge as to the accuracy or otherwise of the report.
Let me make it quite clear that the commissioner was not acting as the Chief Justice of Canada. He was a royal commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act and, as such, his report is not immune from criticism or discussion. There is ample precedent for that; there is ample precedent right in this parliament. If hon. members want any confirmation of that statement, let me say that during the last war there was a shell inquiry presided over by Sir William Meredith, Chief Justice of Ontario, and Mr. Justice Duff, as commissioners, and the Liberal party of that day tried to tear that report to pieces-with what success I do not know; I was not here at the time. Again, during the last war Lord Cromer and his associates made a report in Great Britain, and after a four-hour debate in the British parliament, what was the result? The investigation was with respect to the Gallipoli campaign. An attack was made on the report of that royal commission by Mr. Asquith, who was then Prime Minister of Great Britain, and by no less a person than Mr. Winston Churchill, the present British Prime Minister, and in Mr. Asquith's memoirs will be found this statement. I am not quoting verbatim, but I believe my memory is correct. He said that after four hours' discussion of the Cromer report there was nothing left of it.
That is correct.

Now we come to this report. The report was brought down, and the evidence was refused on the ground that the hearing had been held in secret. That hearing must have been held in secret on the motion of the government, or the government would never have passed the order in council of March 2, the contents of which I never heard of until to-night-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It was not.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury); -and which I would have protested against. I did protest in one quarter against the proceedings being
[Mr R. B. Hanson.]
in secret. I admitted that there were certain portions of the hearing which probably ought to be in secret, and I referred to intergovernmental communications to which there were two parties, one party being this government, and the other the government of the United Kingdom. Those communications could not be made public without the consent of -the British government. However, the inquiry went on in secret. The report was made. A question was raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) as to an opportunity being given to discuss that report in this House of Commons. I had not asked for that because I felt that to discuss that report without the evidence would be perfectly useless, that we could not have an honest, intelligent discussion of the report unless we had the evidence. We have a report which is the interpretation of a commissioner as to the evidence produced before him. On the point of this report being sacrosanct, it is in no other category than the judgment of a court of law from which I as counsel might appeal. I might appeal from the judge's interpretation of the law as applied to the evidence, and that is done in the courts of the country every day, every week, every month. My hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston),
I myself, and every other lawyer practising at the bar have to do that. It does not mean an attack on the judge. It means an attack on the findings, on the interpretation of the judge, and that is open to any counsel; otherwise, there would never be an appeal. To say that this report cannot be criticized-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No one is saying that.

Let me develop my argument. To say that this report cannot be criticized is beside the mark. But how can one criticize the report if he has not the evidence upon which it is based? I submit that it is in the public interest, in the national interest, that this evidence should be laid on the table and that the Canadian public should have it. Without that evidence no discussion, no argument, based solely on the report itself, can be complete. It will be wholly unsatisfactory not only to those who make the attempt to discuss the report, but to the Canadian people, because the facts upon which the report is based are not disclosed to the country. It is not in the national interest that this thing should be kept secret. I protest against that decision.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar rose in his place one day this week. He had received from Colonel Drew, as I had, a copy of his letter to the Prime Minister. The

Hong Kong Commission
hon. member made a perfectly natural request that the letter be tabled, in order that it might become a public document. Until it is tabled it is not a public document. It is a communication from one individual to another, although the latter may be the Prime Minister, but until it is tabled it is not a public document. That was the position.
Immediately the Prime Minister said he would table the letter, if-and he predicated his statement on this "if"-the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would take the responsibility of asking for it. I queried in my own mind at the time why it was predicated on that condition. Was it an attempt to intimidate the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, to make him responsible for the contents of the letter? I do not know. But I took occasion to look into the matter later, and I say that in my opinion there was no responsibility resting on the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he asked that the letter, of which he had a copy, be tabled in order that it might become a public document.
Second thoughts have now occasioned a reversal of the position which the Prime Minister took. What has happened in the meantime? I gave out no copy of this letter to any newspaper, but I was informed within the last hour that a press agency in this country has carried a large portion, if not the whole, of this letter to the public press in Canada; that thousands of newspaper employees from one end of this country to the other know the contents of this letter; that it is now in fact, if not de jure, in the hands of the public. All that remains is to release the obligation imposed on the press agency which gave the letter to the newspapers that it should not be released until the document had been tabled.
The Prime Minister now refuses to table the document. I think he is within his rights in doing so; it was a letter from one individual to another. But let the public have this letter, let the chips fall where they may; I am not responsible for that. The press got the letter from some source, I do not know where and I do not care. They got it in good faith, in the public interest, in order that the public might know what the communication was. Is there any reason why the- public should not know what hundreds of people in this country know, what I know, wha't the Prime Minister knows, what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) know about this matter? If Colonel Drew has transgressed, let Colonel Drew answer. I venture to say he will answer.

Will he answer to the
British government?
Certainly, he takes the responsibility; it is his and his alone. I think he will welcome it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: He will welcome the publicity.

Well, he
is getting it, and the publicity has made him one of the biggest men in Canada, absolutely. What is the position?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Next leader of the Conservative party.

Well, we
might go farther and fare worse.
I say, let us get away from this farce of covering up. Let us have a free press in this country. WTe do not have it. I understand that until the last few minutes there was no censorship on this letter, but I have heard since I came into this chamber to-night that censorship has now been imposed on it. I protest against that in the name of the Canadian people, who want to know the facts and the truth about a great public occurrence. So I ask the Prime Minister to release the censorship, even if he will not table the letter, and let the Canadian people judge. They will judge fairly and truly and accurately, and appraise this incident at its true value. Therefore I ask that the censorship on this letter be released immediately.

When I was asked yesterday if I would assume responsibility for the tabling of this letter I immediately said I would, because I had read the letter' carefully and in my judgment there was nothing in it which would reveal anything of use to the enemy. It was for that reason that I asked for the tabling of the letter. That letter came to me in the ordinary way through the mail. It was not marked confidential or personal or private. It was a copy of a letter addressed to the Prime Minister criticizing in some detail, it is true, the report of the royal commission inquiring into the Hong Kong matter.
This afternoon the Prime Minister showed me the opinion which he has received from Mr. Campbell, the government counsel engaged in the inquiry, advising the Prime Minister that he should withhold the letter. I am not a lawyer, and therefore am not qualified to dispute a legal opinion, and the Prime Minister must take the responsibility for withholding that letter on the advice of counsel. I have no quarrel with the Prime Minister if he believes it is his duty to withhold the letter, although, as I said, in my opinion there is nothing in the letter which
Hong Kong Commission

would be of use to the enemy. On the contrary, I believe that there are matters covered in it which are of interest to the people of Canada and of interest to this parliament. It deals with the dispatch of the expeditionary force to Hong Kong; it makes certain criticisms, criticisms which I believe ought to be known to this parliament in order that this parliament may be guided in the future with regard to the dispatch not of 2,000 men but of many more thousands of men overseas.
One thing that has occurred to me since I was talking to the Prime Minister this afternoon is this. I believe he would have been better advised had he sought an opinion from a counsel who was not interested in this inquiry. I think that obtaining it from a counsel whose integrity is unquestioned but who was engaged in the inquiry was probably a mistake.
As I said before, I am of the opinion that this matter should be gone into. I represent a western constituency, a Saskatchewan constituency. From our prairie constituencies young men went in one of these regiments. Their parents are disturbed by what has occurred; their friends are worried, and those who have sons in other regiments are worried lest repetition of this unfortunate affair should occur. I hold no brief for Colonel Drew or any other person; and since the Prime Minister has stated that it is not in the public interest to produce this letter at this time, not being a lawyer I cannot give a legal opinion upon it. But a great deal has been made of the fact that Sir Lyman P. Duff who made this report is the Chief Justice of Canada.
Sir Lyman P. Duff was not the Chief Justice of Canada when he sat as commissioner. I think the Prime Minister's own statement tonight clearly conveyed that to the house, when he said that the commissioner was vested with the powers of a judge. If he had been sitting as a judge, then manifestly there would have been no need to clothe him further with the powers of a judge. So I think we should keep that aspect entirely out of the discussion.
All I am interested in is endeavouring to bring before parliament in a proper and legitimate manner matters that ought to be discussed here. So I say that as far as I am concerned I asked for the production of the document; I was prepared to ask that it be tabled, as the Prime Minister put it, on my responsibility as a member of this house. Now the Prime Minister, on his responsibility as such, has stated to the house that he is not prepared to submit the document to us, and there, I suppose, unless the house decides otherwise, the matter must rest.
[Mr. Coldwell.3

I have been greatly interested in the question of Hong Kong. I have said very little on the floor of this house concerning the matter, because it seemed hardly wise to say much until one knew more. But I will say that after I received a copy of the letter I went into the question far enough to make one or two discoveries which are of such a nature that I think they certainly should be aired fully somewhere. I am not saying that this should be done on the floor of the house; I am not saying that the information contained in that letter should go out to all the people of the country, with the risk that it might do us harm by getting into the hands of the enemy. I am saying, Mr. Speaker, that in that letter revelations are made of which every member of this house should be fully aware.
There is something wrong in this country, something wrong in the conduct of our military affairs. Whoever was responsible for the blunders that were committed in connection with the dispatch of troops to Hong Kong should be made known to members of this house and should be called upon to answer for those blunders. The cause should be made known, why he committed them; that man should be punished; and such reforms should be made in the set-up concerning the whole conduct of our war effort as would render unlikely a repetition of anything so regrettable as what occurred in connection with the dispatch of those troops.
I am not going to say more. I am not saying, whether or not this letter should be tabled. I am saying that before this house adjourns it is the just right of every constituency in Canada that at least its member should know the whys and wherefores pertaining to this most tragic event in our history.
Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National
Defence): May I say just a word, Mr. Speaker.
I do think some of the remarks that have been made here to-night are, if I may say so, rather premature. There seems to be an assumption that there is to be no opportunity of discussing the Hong Kong expedition. It has been made abundantly clear that there will be ample opportunity for that purpose; and I want to say, as the minister in charge of the department which had to do with the sending of the Hong Kong expedition, that I am perfectly ready to have this house deal with it and consider it as fully as they care to.

Without
the evidence.

My hon. friend says,
"without the evidence." I want to deal with that for just a moment. The situation was-

Hong Kong Commission
this. The right hon. chief justice was appointed a commissioner to examine into the sending of the expedition to Hong Kong. As was stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the time, the commissioner was given absolute power to conduct that inquiry as he saw fit, and no suggestion was made to him in any way by the government with regard to what method he should adopt. He, of his own volition, decided that the inquiry should be held in camera. That decision was not found fault with in the country, because it was realized that there were certain things in connection with the matter which should not be disclosed. Knowing something of the documents and something of the evidence, I can conceive that it would have been hopeless to consider holding a closed session in connection with this document, then an open session in connection with that particular bit of evidence, then going back to a closed session again when a question might be asked later about the first document; it would be absolutely impracticable to conduct the inquiry.
There were two different degrees with regard to secrecy. One was that the general inquiry was held in camera. As I say, the evidence was such that it would be absolutely impossible for a commissioner to deal with it succinctly and properly, and change from time to time from an open session to a closed session as evidence came out on the various points. The whole inquiry was in secret, but there was another point. That was in connection with certain documents which came from the British government. A number of those documents had an additional seal of secrecy on them, to the effect that they could not be even shown or read to those in the courtroom but could be shown only to the commissioner and to counsel. That is the first thing referred to in Mr. Campbell's opinion, which has been read by the Prime Minister. That is all this house is discussing; that is all that has come up so far. What is set out there is this, that the government having requested the British government-and I can assure this house that those requests were in the most unqualified and unreserved terms-to give them permission to produce to the commissioner the communications which passed between the two governments; and having received that permission with certain conditions attached in the case of some documents, namely, that they could be shown only to the commissioner and to counsel, the government now, by tabling a document which has been presented, would be violating that condition and in effect would be saying to the British government, "Although we tendered
those documents to be used for that purpose, at the same time this letter has come to us which indicates the effect of those documents, and we are going to table the letter." What would be our situation with respect to the British government if that were done?
Then with regard to the general rule in regard to the inquiry being held in camera, it was understood, as was indicated there, that all the evidence would be given in camera and would be kept secret. What happens is that the document which is referred to contains, it is said, certain portions of the evidence which were not included in the report of the commissioner; and the government, by tendering and tabling that letter, would itself become a participant in a violation of the conditions which were laid down by the commissioner.
Is the minister referring to the Drew letter?
Yes.
But in the appendix to the report reference is made to the evidence.

Certainly reference is
made to the evidence; and reference is made to all the evidence, I am sure and satisfied, which the commissioner-I will call him the commissioner, but in any event he is the Chief Justice of Canada, with a reputation second to none among jurists on this continent, and with wide judicial knowledge- thought was relevant or necessary to the report. All that evidence is there, and my hon. friend and anybody else in this house have the fullest opportunity to deal with that evidence, to deal with the recital of facts which are given there, and to deal with the whole question as to whether this expedition was properly sent.
Some suggestion has been made that the Roberts commission in the United States did not publish any evidence. The Roberts report did contain reference to evidence from time to time. It did not contain all the evidence. Nobody in the United States ever asked for the rest of the Roberts evidence. They considered that the report was made by commissioners who knew their business, and the result was that that report was accepted.
I am, of course, interested in this matter, and I realize that my view's on this question will be accepted with certain reservations, but I do deprecate the suggestion that somehow or another we should distinguish between a man who is a commissioner at one minute and the Chief Justice of Canada the next
Hong Kong Commission

and consider that he is a different man and of a different calibre and integrity because of the fact that he happens to be in this case a commissioner. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to members of this house that when you have a gentleman of the standing of Sir Lyman Duff selected to hold this inquiry, a selection that was agreed to and approved by everybody who had anything to do with it as being an admirable selection, a man whose reputation is second to none, a man who has been weighing and considering evidence for years and knows how to appreciate evidence, and who was assisted by two eminent counsel from Toronto who had nothing to do with the' government whatever, by Mr. Campbell of Montreal, and by Colonel Drew representing the leader of the opposition, it seems to me that the public of Canada and, I would suggest, even this house have a right to consider that this matter, which was gone into for five or six weeks, has been pretty fully investigated and that the findings can fairly be taken as the findings of disinterested men. However, that will come later. I could not help saying that, when I heard this distinction being made between the chief justice and the commissioner because, after all, it is one and the same individual who made these findings whose findings are now being questioned.
My hon. friend mentioned the order in council of March 2. He says he did not know anything about it.

Not at the
time it was passed.

All I have to say is that the extract read from the record to-night indicates that the operative part of the order in council was read to counsel whom my hon. friend nominated on the 4th day of March.
I would not dispute that. I never attended the meetings.

My hon. friend seems to suggest that there was some covering up of_ this order in council. The order in council was read, and the extract is there indicating that.
I had not intended to take any part in this matter, but I did feel that it was due to me and due to the department I represent that the house should realize that this matter has been investigated and, I think, most thoroughly.
I want to say to my hon. friend the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) that he will have full opportunity to deal with the sweeping statements which he made in connection

with this matter, and I trust that I shall also have an opportnuity of saying a word or two. I ask him not to get completely out of focus in connection with this matter simply because of the fact that the gentleman who happened to be counsel and who acted as prosecuting counsel and does not appear to be satisfied with the judgment which was rendered in this case, sees fit to write to the Prime Minister a letter, which letter is not being tabled. I am sure that that letter is in the hands of a great many hon. members, and I am sure that they can use the arguments put forward there to their hearts' content, and make them their own. But I do suggest that the government is taking the only course it can take in not tabling the communication, because to do so would be a direct breach of the conditions imposed by the British government, and a direct breach of the conditions imposed by the commissioner at the time he opened the inquiry.
I said a moment ago that it was indicated that the public generally were in favour of this inquiry and saw the necessity of the inquiry being conducted in secret. I happen to have in my hand an editorial from the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 26, which states:
A royal commission to inquire into the circumstances surrounding the debacle at Hong Ivong will shortly sit to hear the evidence. The inquiry will be held in camera, and several letters of complaint have been addressed to this newspaper from readers who believe that the proceedings should be open to the public. In view' of the nature of the inquiry and the extent to "which details of production, organization, transport and kindred matters are likely to be produced in evidence, it is obvious that the public cannot possibly be admitted. In order that the commissioner may write a just account of the episode, placing blame where it is due, exonerating those who have been unreasonably blamed, and attributing to material factors their proper share in producing the final result, it will be necessary for him to hear many things which the enemy would like to know'. It is therefore not merely justifiable but imperative that evidence be heard in secret.

Mr. Speaker, my first word will be in answer to this laughter in which some hon. members are indulging. I represent a constituency which furnished [DOT] a very large number of the young men who were sent with the Royal Rifle Regiment to Hong Kong, and therefore I think I have a right to say a few words on the subject without laughter from some hon. gentlemen. My constituency, up to date, has given to the country the largest number of volunteers of all the constituencies of Ganada.
I shall be very brief in my remarks. The decision reached by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to-night will be a great

Hong Kong Commission
disappointment to the families of my constituency who are expecting to hear some explanation of the circumstances of this expedition to Hong Kong. Apparently, however, they will have to accept the decision which has been taken by the government that neither the evidence taken at the inquiry nor Mr. Drew's letter will be made public. That action will surely leave an uneasy feeling throughout the country. I would suggest that there seems to be a very easy way in which to satisfy everybody, at least the people's representatives in this house. It would be to bring up these matters before parliament in a secret session together with the important question of enemy activities in the St. Lawrence river. That course seems to me the best way in which to settle this difficulty of informing the members without risk of anything going abroad.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) began his remarks by taking exception to an order in council from which I read as one which he said had not previously been presented either to the house or to himself. To be exact, P.C. 1369, the order in council which I read, was tabled in this house on April 21 and has been before the house ever since. But apart from that, as my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has just stated, the effective part of the order in council was read to counsel by the chief justice himself at the time the inquiry was held. Counsel for my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was fully aware of all that was contained in the order, and I should be greatly surprised if he did not communicate the contents of it to my hon. friend.
The leader of the opposition assumes-I think he went even farther-and alleged that the inquiry was held in secret at the instance of the government. My hon. friend knows that that is not the case, because early in this session he himself brought up the subject of secrecy, and I made it very clear at the time that the question of whether the inquiry was to be held in camera would rest entirely with the chief justice; that I had made it abundantly clear to the chief justice that the government wished to place no restriction of any kind upon him or to give him a direction of any kind, and that the reason why he was being selected as commissioner was that as Chief Justice of Canada we believed that there was no man in Canada in whose integrity and sound judgment the people of Canada had more complete faith and confidence.
On February 19,1942, my hon. friend brought up the question of secrecy. He stated that he
had not had any confirmation as to whether the inquiry was to be in secret, but he understood
that it was. I quote from page 705 of Hansard:
Mr. Hanson 'York-Sunbury): I assume it is;
I have not had confirmation from the chief justice.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	I assume it is, too.
Neither of us apparently is aware of the facts. However, at the time I asked the chief justice if he would unuertake the inquiry I gave him the assurance that the government would not wish to restrict him in any particular, and that it would be for him to decide how the proceedings should be conducted, what assistance he would require in connection with the conduct of the proceedings, and in fact all matters with respect to the commission. I assume if the chief justice has decided to hold the sittings of the commission in secret, as was the case with the United States inquiry into conditions at Pearl Harbour, he has evidently had the best of reasons for so doing. I do not know that I can say more than that.
I think that should dispose once and for all of the question as to whether the chief justice acted entirely on his own and in what he believed- to be the best interests of the country and of all parties concerned, and as to his not having had any direction, either directly or indirectly, from the government with respect to any part of the proceedings.
In reference to the letter under discussion being tabled, may I say that as the leader of the house I have felt a special responsibility with respect to preventing any attacks or anything in the nature of an attack on or an insinuation about anyone in a judicial position coming directly or indirectly from any part of this house. When I read the letter that came from Mr. Drew I had in mind very much the rules of this house with respect to what was and what was not proper in the course of debate. I leave it to the three hon. gentlemen who have read this letter to say whether they agree or disagree with me when I say that in that letter are statements which could not be construed, as far as I can see, in any way other than as a most serious reflection upon the commissioner, who is the chief justice of this country. I should like to quote citation 305 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms as follows:
All references to judges and courts of justice and to personages of high official station, of the nature of personal attack and censure have always been considered unparliamentary, and the Speakers of the British and Canadian houses have always treated them as breaches of order. Members have even been interrupted in committees of the whole by the Chairman when they have cast an imputation upon a judicial proceeding. The proper course for persons who feel called upon to attack the conduct of a judge is to proceed by way of a petition in which all the allegations are specifically stated so that the person accused may have full opportunity to answer the charges presented against him.

Hong Kong Commission

I may say to my hon. friend that the worst feature of the letter which I read was the imputation which it seemed to me it cast upon the judgment and, I would equally say, the integrity of the commissioner who is the chief justice of this country. May I add the fact that our chief justice, in the person of Sir Lyman Duff, is not only a member of the privy council of this country; he is a member of the judicial committee of the privy council of the United Kingdom, and no member of that body is held in greater respect in any part of the world. It seems to me that it would be impossible to have this communication tabled without one being a party to imputations upon the integrity and honour and good judgment of the chief justice of this country.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition spoke about censorship and said that he thought I should take steps immediately to relieve the censors of some ruling which they have given. I have not interfered with the censorship at any time, and I do not intend to do so at this time.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said that one exception he would take to my course in seeking legal opinion was that I had not consulted some counsel other than the particular counsel chosen. There were, among others, two reasons in particular for the choice of Mr. George Campbell. The first was that Mr. Campbell, as counsel for the government on the commission, was in a position to know the conditions under which the evidence was given, communications produced, and all circumstances surrounding the inquiry. If I had sought legal opinion outside of the counsel who had appeared before the commission, no one would have been able to state with definite knowledge what the limitations and the restrictions and the undertakings were. I think that of itself is a sufficient answer. I would say further, I believe this house will agree that few if any counsel in Canada have a higher reputation for integrity and ability than has Mr. Campbell, who was counsel for the government in this inquiry.
Just a word in conclusion as to the withholding of this letter. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke of it as being withheld in the public interest. I have never given that as a reason for its not being tabled. I have said I did not "wish that this house or anyone connected with it should be a party to violating the conditions under which some of the information in the report was given before the commission. The undertaking by the government to the British government which governed the conditions under which

[DOT]certain communications were placed before the commission and considered by the chief justice and the counsel who appeared before the commission was not an undertaking of one government to another as such; it was an undertaking by Canada to the United Kingdom, the government acting as the representative of this country. I mention that because I feel that this House of Commons, representing the people of Canada, would not wish to be a party or have any of its members a party to the violation of any undertaking or agreements which existed between the governments of the two countries.

May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question just to clear up one point, since I read the letter and take the responsibility for asking that it be tabled? The right hon. gentleman has given the impression, I think, that Colonel Drew quoted from documents passing between the government of Canada and the British government. I do not think that is so. My recollection is that he referred to certain matters but that there were no documents given and no quotations from them.

Quite
right.

May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question. Under the public inquiries act must not a commission-

-conduct proceedings in public? That is the law, by statute and usage and custom.
Order.

I remember that an opinion was given to me years ago by, I believe, the Department of Justice. An inquiry under the Inquiries Act is a public proceeding. I should like to get an answer, Mr. Speaker. I moved for these papers last Wednesday.
